The Pink cockatoo (Lophochroa leadbeateri) is a medium-sized Australian parrot that exhibits striking sexual dimorphism in body mass, with adult males regularly attaining larger sizes than females. Field measurements indicate that the maximum adult body mass for females reaches approximately 392 grams [Wwi = approximately 392 grams], while males can achieve a significantly greater ultimate wet weight of around 424 grams [Wwi = around 424 grams]. This difference is thought to reflect the energetic demands of male-male competition for nest hollows in the arid and semi-arid regions they inhabit. Neonatal mass at hatching is comparatively modest, with newly emerged chicks typically weighing about 12 grams [Wwb = about 12 grams], a value that aligns with the altricial developmental mode characteristic of most psittaciforms. Early growth is rapid, though initial wet weights at the very onset of development have been reported as 15.3 grams [Ww0 = 15.3 grams] in some captive-rearing studies, slightly greater than the 11 grams cited by Carv2008 from a wild population. This variation likely reflects differences in maternal condition or egg size across the species’ geographic range.

Under controlled incubation conditions of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], the age at hatching for this species is approximately 25 days [ab = approximately 25 days], though field records document a broader range of 23 to 30 days depending on ambient thermal regimes. The incubation period is consistent with that of other Cacatuidae of comparable body size, where prolonged egg attendance is necessary for the successful development of the large-yolked, calcareous egg. The temperature of 36 °C appears to represent an optimal mean for embryogenesis, with deviations outside this range leading to increased mortality or developmental abnormalities. Once hatched, the altricial nestling enters a phase of rapid mass gain and feather development, entirely dependent on bi-parental provisioning. The initial wet weight of the hatchling, documented at 15.3 grams [Ww0 = 15.3 grams] in captive cohorts, provides a baseline from which growth trajectories are measured against adult asymptotic mass values.

When reared under a thermal environment of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C], characteristic of the core body temperatures maintained during active periods, the developmental schedule of the Pink cockatoo follows a well-defined sequence. Fledging, defined as the achievement of sustained flight and departure from the nest cavity, occurs at approximately 57.5 days after hatching [tx = approximately 57.5 days after hatching] at a temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]. This relatively extended nestling period is typical of larger cockatoos and is thought to be necessary for the full development of flight feathers and neuromuscular coordination required for predator evasion in open woodland habitats. The timing of fledging is a critical life-history transition; chicks that leave the nest too early face high mortality from predation, while those that remain too long may deplete parental resources. Observations at 41.3 °C in captive aviaries confirm that this temperature regime supports normal fledging without heat stress complications.

Sexual maturation in Lophochroa leadbeateri occurs well after the fledgling stage, with puberty estimated at 172.5 days after birth [tp = estimated at 172.5 days after birth] under conditions maintained at 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]. This relatively delayed onset of reproductive capability, compared to smaller parrot species, is consistent with a life-history strategy that prioritizes extensive somatic growth and social learning before first breeding. First-year birds often associate in loose juvenile flocks before pairing, and gonadal activation is thought to be influenced by photoperiod and food availability rather than thermal cues alone. The ultimate body mass of adult females at approximately 392 grams [Wwi = approximately 392 grams] and males at 424 grams [Wwi = 424 grams] is typically attained before or during this pubertal transition, indicating that a threshold of structural size must be reached before reproductive physiology commences. Available data from long-term captive populations suggest that the interval between hatching and sexual maturity is remarkably consistent when ambient temperatures are held near 41.3 °C.

Under sustained thermal conditions of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C], first breeding in the Pink cockatoo is typically deferred until approximately 3 years since birth [tR = approximately 3 years since birth], with some individuals commencing reproduction as early as 3 years of age. The reproductive output during each nesting attempt is modest, with females laying approximately 3.29 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 3.29 eggs per clutch], and typically producing a single brood each year [F_R_i = single brood each year], which corresponds to a maximum daily reproduction rate of approximately 0.009 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 0.009 eggs per day] at 41.3 °C. This low annual reproductive rate is compensated by an extended maximum lifespan, with the oldest documented wild individuals reaching approximately 77 years [am = approximately 77 years], a longevity that permits multiple breeding opportunities across a lifetime at a temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]. The maximum lifespan of approximately 77 years [am = approximately 77 years] places Lophochroa leadbeateri among the longer-lived parrots, a trait often linked to low extrinsic adult mortality in stable, arid-zone environments at a temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]. Comparative data from related cockatoo species suggest that such extreme lifespans are facilitated by a slow-paced life history, where delayed reproduction and high adult survival are favored.
